items.explanation_markdown:
You bought a new pair of shoes. They were on sale, the color was exactly what you wanted, and you walked out of the store feeling like you'd won. Less than a week later, the sole peels off the left one while you're crossing the street.

```jp
{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kutsu||靴[くつ]}}を{{kau-v|ta|買[か]った}}。{{totemo||とても}}{{yasui-adj|ta|安[やす]かった}}。
ところが、{{sugu||すぐ}}に{{kowareru|ta|壊[こわ]れた}}。
```
*I bought new shoes. They were very cheap.*
*However, they broke right away.*

That third line is where ところが earns its keep. The first two sentences built up an expectation — new shoes, a good price, nothing to complain about — and then ところが yanks the story somewhere you didn't see coming. That's the whole job of this word: it marks the exact point where a situation you thought you understood turns out to have a catch.

It's tempting to translate ところが as a plain "but," and most dictionaries will hand you exactly that gloss. It isn't wrong, but it undersells what's happening. "But" can join two facts that were never expected to line up in the first place — "the shoes were cheap, but I don't really like the color" is a mild, low-stakes "but." ところが is reserved for the moment the story actively double-crosses you. If nobody would raise an eyebrow at your sentence, ところが is probably too strong a word for it.

## How it works

ところが sits at the front of its own sentence, right after the full stop of the sentence before it. Nothing about that first sentence changes shape to make room for it — no special ending, no attaching to a verb stem, no plain-form requirement the way something like か{{dou||どう}}か demands. You finish your first sentence normally, in whatever form you'd already use — plain or polite, past or present — then start a fresh sentence with ところが, drop a comma, and say what actually happened.

```jp
{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{resutoran||レストラン}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
ところが、{{nedan||値[ね]段[だん]}}が{{totemo||とても}}{{takai-adj|ta|高[たか]かった}}。
```
*I went to a new restaurant.*
*However, the price was very expensive.*

The shape is always: Sentence. + ところが、+ Sentence. Because ところが is doing all the connecting work by itself, it never needs help from another word — you won't see it stacked onto something else in the same slot. It stands alone, and it always opens the sentence that carries the surprise, never the one that sets it up.

It also doesn't care what kind of sentence it's attaching to. The first half can end in a verb, an adjective, or a noun-plus-copula, in plain speech or polite speech, and ところが sits down after it exactly the same way every time. Compare that to something like か{{dou||どう}}か, which only accepts a plain-form verb or adjective right before it and rejects です outright — ところが has no such restriction, because it isn't attaching to anything at all. It's standing at the start of a brand-new sentence, looking back at the one that just ended.

## Rules and exceptions

ところが wants something that actually happened — a real event you're reporting on, usually a first half in the past tense that turned out to be a setup for a second half nobody predicted. It isn't built for hedging about the future or floating a plan that might fall through; it's for telling someone what did happen, and how it didn't go the way the first sentence implied.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}を{{eki||駅[えき]}}で{{matsu|ta|待[ま]った}}。
ところが、{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}は{{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]なかった}}。
```
*I waited for my friend at the station.*
*However, my friend didn't come.*

> Use ところが on two facts that were never actually in tension with each other and it reads like a plot twist that never arrives — the listener braces for a reversal and gets a shrug instead. Save it for a moment where something genuinely goes sideways; if nothing sideways happened, a plain connecting word does the job better.

Real speech is a little messier than that rule makes it sound. You'll hear ところが used in narration, news reports, and casual storytelling even when the "surprise" is fairly mild — more of a scene-turn than a shock. Don't fight that texture too hard while you're still getting a feel for it; leaning toward genuine reversal is the safer habit to build first, and the softer, everyday uses will come naturally once the core sense is solid.

This one is worth sitting with, because you already have the instinct for it in English — you say "but then" or "except" in exactly this spot without thinking. The only new muscle is remembering that in Japanese, that pivot word starts its own sentence instead of getting stitched onto the end of the one before it.

There's also a habit worth building around who ところが is allowed to surprise. It almost always describes something happening to the speaker, or something the speaker is reporting on as an outside observer — not a plan the speaker themselves is still deciding on. If you haven't lived through the twist yet, or you're only guessing that something might go wrong, ところが is the wrong tool; you'd want a different, more tentative way of talking about it. ところが speaks with the confidence of someone describing something that's already over and done.

## Contrast: ところが vs. 反[はん]面[めん]

You've already met 反[はん]面[めん] for holding two sides of the same thing up against each other — a "while at the same time" kind of contrast. It's built for describing standing qualities, not for narrating an event that overturned what you expected.

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{kibishii||厳[きび]しい}}反[はん]面[めん]、{{yasashii-n4||優[やさ]しい}}。
```
*My older brother is strict, while also being kind.*

That sentence is a portrait: two traits that sit side by side in the same person, all the time, with nothing surprising about either one. ところが needs something different — a timeline, a before and an after, something that was true and then, unexpectedly, stopped being true.

It helps to notice that 反[はん]面[めん] sentences usually still make sense if you flip the order — "strict while also kind" and "kind while also strict" describe the same person either way. Try that with ところが and it breaks immediately: "always strict, however today kind" tells a specific story in a specific direction, and reversing it — "kind today, however always strict" — describes someone completely different. That directionality is the real fingerprint of ところが. It isn't just joining two ideas; it's insisting that the second one landed as a surprise given the first.

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{itsumo||いつも}}{{kibishii||厳[きび]しい}}。
ところが、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yasashii-n4|ta|優[やさ]しかった}}。
```
*My older brother is always strict.*
*However, today he was kind.*

Same brother, the same two qualities even, but now there's a story: always strict, until today, when he wasn't. Try swapping in 反[はん]面[めん] here and the sentence falls apart — 反[はん]面[めん] doesn't know what to do with "today" breaking a pattern; all it knows how to do is hold two sides of one unchanging picture at once.

That's the test you can run in your head. If the honest next question is "and then what happened?" and the answer overturns the first half, reach for ところが. If you're just describing two sides of the same coin with no event involved, 反[はん]面[めん] is the better tool.

Neither of them is right or wrong in some absolute sense — they're answering different questions. 反[はん]面[めん] answers "what is this thing like?" ところが answers "what happened, and how did it not go the way it looked like it would?" Once you can hear that difference, mixing them up gets a lot harder to do by accident.

Hold onto that distinction — {{sorede||それで}}も lives in the same neighborhood, for the moments later on when the surprise doesn't end the story, it just makes whatever comes next harder to pull off.
caution_notes: ところが needs a genuine turn of events; using it to link two facts that were never in tension just sounds like a false alarm.
Nothing about the first sentence changes form for ところが — it simply opens the next sentence on its own, followed by a comma.
ところが reports something that already happened, so don't reach for it to hedge about a future plan or an unconfirmed guess.
反面 holds two qualities of one thing at the same time; ところが needs a before-and-after where the first part gets overturned, so the two aren't interchangeable.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you moved to Tokyo three years ago, and someone at a party asks how long you've been in Japan. You could just give a number, but what you actually want to say is "ever since I got here, I've been living in this city" — one clause that ties the moment you arrived to everything that has been true since. That job belongs to 以[い]来[らい] (いらい), literally "since."

## How it works

以[い]来[らい] attaches directly to a noun that names a point in time, or to the te-form of a verb (the -て form — the connecting shape you already use for "and" and for requests). Either way, it marks the moment something started, and everything after it in the sentence describes what has stayed true from that moment up to right now.

With a verb, you first build the te-form, then add 以[い]来[らい] right after it.

```jp
{{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{kuru-v|te|来[き]て}}
```

*to come → having come*

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{kuru-v|te|来[き]て}}以[い]来[らい]、{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}です。
```

*Ever since I came to Japan, I've been busy every day.*

Look at the shape: [action in te-form] + 以[い]来[らい] + [ongoing state]. The second half is never a one-time event — it's something that has kept being true since the te-form clause happened. That's the whole engine of 以[い]来[らい]: a starting line, then an unbroken stretch of time after it, right up to the present.

The same mechanic works for {{suru||する}}-verbs, where the te-form is 〜{{suru|te|して}}.

```jp
{{sotsugyou-suru||卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]する}} → {{v-sotsugyou||卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]}}して
```

*to graduate → having graduated*

```jp
{{v-sotsugyou||卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]}}して以[い]来[らい]、{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{au|te|会[あ]って}}{{iru-exist|masu|いません}}。
```

*I haven't seen my teacher since I graduated.*

With a noun, you skip the te-form entirely and attach 以[い]来[らい] straight to the time word — no verb needed at all.

```jp
{{sengetsu||先[せん]月[げつ]}}以[い]来[らい]、{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}です。
```

*I've been sick since last month.*

That's the whole mechanic, in two shapes: noun + 以[い]来[らい], or verb-te-form + 以[い]来[らい], always followed by something ongoing.

## Rules and exceptions

以[い]来[らい] is built for change that sticks. If nothing has been continuously true since the starting point, 以[い]来[らい] is the wrong tool — it doesn't just mean "at some point after X," it means "from X, unbroken, until right now."

```jp
{{v-kekkon||結[けっ]婚[こん]}}して以[い]来[らい]、{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}を{{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*Ever since I got married, I've been cooking every day.*

> Only the て-form works here — a plain past tense like `来た以来` is not something you'll hear native speakers use. If you can build the て-form, you can use 以[い]来[らい]; if you're reaching for 〜た, stop and switch back to 〜て.

The other trap is scale. 以[い]来[らい] wants a starting point big enough to carry a stretch of time after it — a life event, a season, a named date — not a five-minute gap. Nobody reaches for 以[い]来[らい] over something that small; that's what plain て-form clauses without 以[い]来[らい] are for.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}が{{umareru|te|生[う]まれて}}以[い]来[らい]、{{amari||あまり}}{{neru|te|寝[ね]て}}{{iru-exist|masu|いません}}。
```

*Ever since our child was born, I haven't slept much.*

This one trips people the first week, because English "since" covers both jobs — the one-off "since Tuesday I've been at my desk" and the reason-giving "since you're here, help me" — and only the first of those is 以[い]来[らい]'s job. The second is a completely different word, and mixing them up is a very natural mistake to make early on.

## Contrast

You already know 以[い]外[がい] (except / other than), and it's an easy one to misread at a glance — both words start with 以[い], and both feel like they're marking some kind of boundary. But 以[い]外[がい] draws a line around what's excluded from a group; it has nothing to do with time at all.

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{wakaru|masu|分[わ]かりません}}。
```

*I don't understand anything except Japanese.*

{{sono||その}}ため is a different kind of neighbor: it links a cause to its result — that happened, so this happened — while 以[い]来[らい] links a starting point to everything that has followed it. {{sono||その}}ため cares about *why* something happened; 以[い]来[らい] cares about *since when* something has been true.

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}に{{naru-become|masu|なりました}}。{{sono||その}}ため、{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}を{{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}}ました。
```

*I got sick. Because of that, I took the day off work.*

Swap 以[い]来[らい] in for {{sono||その}}ため there and the sentence stops making sense — "sick, and 以[い]来[らい] I took the day off" throws away the cause-and-effect link that {{sono||その}}ため was carrying, and replaces it with a claim about an ongoing state that was never there.

以[い]来[らい] opens a sentence by naming when an ongoing state began. Hold onto that starting-point feeling — it comes back when you meet {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}}に, which flips a situation around instead of anchoring it in time.
caution_notes: 以来 needs a te-form verb or a time noun in front of it — a plain past tense like 来た以来 is not a form native speakers use, so use 来て以来 instead.
以来 marks an unbroken ongoing state that continues to the present, not a single one-off event somewhere in the past.
以来 and 以外 look alike but are unrelated — 以外 marks exclusion from a group, not a point in time.
以来 fits a starting point big enough to carry a stretch of time after it, like a life event or a named date, not a five-minute gap.

items.explanation_markdown:
You tell a friend the forecast said sun today, then you step outside straight into rain. That gap — between what you expected and what actually happened — needs its own word in Japanese, and that word is 反[はん]対[たい]に (はんたいに), "on the contrary" or "conversely." It doesn't soften bad news, and it doesn't add a reason for anything. It just flags a flat reversal: you thought one thing, reality delivered the opposite.

You'll hear 反[はん]対[たい]に just as often in conversation as you'll see it in writing — it's not a stiff, bookish word. Someone recapping their day, correcting a guess you made, or comparing two people's reactions will reach for it naturally, the same way you'd reach for "on the contrary" in English without thinking twice.

## How it works

反[はん]対[たい]に is built from the noun {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}} (the opposite, or opposition) plus the particle に — the same に that turns a lot of nouns into adverbs, the way {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}} becomes {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}に or {{jiyuu||自[じ]由[ゆう]}} becomes {{jiyuu||自[じ]由[ゆう]}}に. Once you see that seam, the meaning falls out naturally: {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}} is "the opposite thing," so 反[はん]対[たい]に is "in the opposite way."

```jp
{{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}} → 反[はん]対[たい]に
```

The structure is simple: 反[はん]対[たい]に sits in front of the statement that carries the reversal. Everything before it sets up an expectation — a guess, a plan, a prediction — and everything after 反[はん]対[たい]に knocks that expectation down.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{atsui-hot||暑[あつ]い}}と{{omou|ta|思[おも]った}}。
反[はん]対[たい]に、{{totemo||とても}}{{samui|ta|寒[さむ]かった}}。
```
*I thought today would be hot.*
*On the contrary, it was very cold.*

You'll almost always see a comma right after 反[はん]対[たい]に in writing. It isn't required by any rule, but it marks the small pause before the reversal lands, and nearly everyone writes it that way. 反[はん]対[たい]に also shows up mid-sentence, right after a contrasting が or けど, doing the exact same job without starting a new sentence:

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}と{{iu-v|ta|言[い]った}}が、反[はん]対[たい]に{{hima||暇[ひま]}}だった。
```
*He said he was busy, but on the contrary he was free.*

Here's the part that trips people up the first week: 反[はん]対[たい]に never conjugates. It isn't an adjective bending through forms, and it isn't a verb taking a tense. It sits frozen, exactly as you see it, whether the sentence around it is past, present, polite, or plain — only the sentence *following* 反[はん]対[たい]に carries tense and politeness.

That frozen shape is also what separates 反[はん]対[たい]に from the bare noun {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}}, which does show up on its own and means "opposed" or "against" — someone's stance, not a reversal of an expectation.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{sono||その}}{{hanashi||話[はなし]}}に{{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}}だ。
```
*She is against that story.*

That sentence never sets up something to flip; it just states a position. 反[はん]対[たい]に only earns its place when the sentence has a "you'd think X, but actually Y" shape underneath it — no setup, no job for 反[はん]対[たい]に to do.

You'll also spot plain {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}} sitting in front of a noun with の, as in {{hantai||反[はん]対[たい]}}の{{iken||意[い]見[けん]}} (the opposing opinion). That's still the ordinary noun doing ordinary noun-modification work — describing which opinion, not flipping a whole sentence — so don't let the shared kanji fool you into treating it like 反[はん]対[たい]に.

There's also a difference in *scope* worth noticing. 反[はん]対[たい]に reaches across the whole clause that follows it, not just the next word. In 反[はん]対[たい]に、{{totemo||とても}}{{samui|ta|寒[さむ]かった}} above, the reversal covers "it was very cold" as a complete idea — not just {{samui|ta|寒[さむ]かった}} in isolation. That's part of why it can't glue onto a single adjective or verb the way a suffix would; it needs a full statement on the other side to reverse.

## Rules and exceptions

反[はん]対[たい]に needs two sides to work: the assumption, stated or implied, and the reversal it introduces. Drop the setup entirely and 反[はん]対[たい]に reads like a connector with nothing to connect — a reversal of nothing in particular.

> Don't reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に just because two facts happen to differ. It marks a genuine flip — heat turning to cold, "easy" turning into "hard" — not a second, unrelated detail tacked onto the first sentence.

This is also why 反[はん]対[たい]に almost never opens a conversation cold. It leans on something already said or already assumed — a forecast, a rumor, a first impression — and answers it. Say it with nothing behind it and a listener will wait for the part they missed, the expectation you're supposedly correcting.

A common beginner slip is trying to fuse 反[はん]対[たい]に directly onto the word before it, as if it were a suffix, something like `暑い反対に`. That's not how it behaves: 反[はん]対[たい]に always stands alone at the head of its own clause, never glued onto the adjective or verb next to it.

```jp
{{tesuto||テスト}}は{{kantan-n4||簡[かん]単[たん]}}だと{{omou|ta|思[おも]った}}が、反[はん]対[たい]に{{totemo||とても}}{{muzukashii|ta|難[むずか]しかった}}。
```
*I thought the test would be easy, but on the contrary it was very difficult.*

Notice that the two halves genuinely oppose each other — {{kantan-n4||簡[かん]単[たん]}} and {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} are opposite qualities, not just two facts that happen to sit in the same sentence. That's the test worth running before you commit to 反[はん]対[たい]に: can you state the flipped expectation as a clean opposite? If not, a plain {{demo||でも}} or {{shikashi||しかし}} usually fits the sentence better.

It also helps to know what 反[はん]対[たい]に is *not* doing. It never explains a cause the way {{sono||その}}ため does — {{sono||その}}ため links a reason to its result ("it rained, so the game was cancelled"), while 反[はん]対[たい]に never tells you why anything happened. It only reports that the outcome ended up facing the other direction from what you expected. Reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に when you want to correct an assumption, not when you want to justify an outcome.

## Contrast: 反[はん]対[たい]に vs {{sorede||それで}}も

You already know {{sorede||それで}}も for "even so" — it keeps an action going despite an obstacle, without changing what actually happened. 反[はん]対[たい]に is a different animal entirely: it says the actual result flipped to the other side, not that something pushed through in spite of it.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。
{{sorede||それで}}も、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{sanpo-suru|ta|散[さん]歩[ぽ]した}}。
```
*It was raining.*
*Even so, he went for a walk.*

Here the rain never stopped, and the walk happened anyway — {{sorede||それで}}も just reports that the plan survived the obstacle. Now compare a scenario where the obstacle itself turns out to be the wrong guess:

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}}と{{omou|ta|思[おも]った}}。
反[はん]対[たい]に、{{ii||いい}}{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}に{{naru-become|ta|なった}}。
```
*I thought it would rain.*
*On the contrary, it turned into good weather.*

No walk, no obstacle overcome — the rain simply never happened, and something else took its place. That's the test to run in your head: if the expected thing still occurred and something pushed through it anyway, reach for {{sorede||それで}}も. If the expected thing just didn't happen, and its opposite did instead, reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に.

Swap the two connectors in either sentence above and you'd be describing a different day entirely. {{sorede||それで}}も in the second sentence would claim the rain came and someone still got good weather out of it, which makes no sense — the two facts can't coexist. That's the giveaway that these aren't stylistic alternatives; they're built for opposite jobs.

Predictions are wrong all the time — the weather, someone's mood, how a test goes. Now you have the word for saying so plainly, no hedging and no soft landing, just 反[はん]対[たい]に and the truth.

One habit worth building now: before you write 反[はん]対[たい]に, say the expectation out loud first, even silently. If you can't finish the sentence "I thought ___" before it, there's nothing for 反[はん]対[たい]に to reverse, and the sentence probably wants {{demo||でも}}, {{shikashi||しかし}}, or {{sorede||それで}}も instead. That one-second check is the whole rule, and it holds up in every example in this lesson.
caution_notes: 反対に needs a stated or implied expectation before it — without one, it has nothing to reverse and reads like an empty connector.
Don't confuse 反対に with bare 反対, which just states someone's opposition (話に反対だ) rather than reversing an expectation.
反対に never conjugates and never fuses onto the word before it — avoid a form like 暑い反対に.
反対に flips an outcome; it doesn't explain a cause, so don't use it where そのため (reason → result) is what you actually mean.

items.explanation_markdown:
You just moved apartments, and your friend spent the whole weekend hauling boxes, assembling furniture, and hanging your curtains while you mostly stood around handing them things. When they thank *you* for the help, you need to correct the record — fast, and with feeling. Plain Japanese has a word for exactly this job: こそ.

```jp
{{anata||あなた}}こそ{{ganbaru|masu|頑[がん]張[ば]りました}}。
```

*You're the one who really worked hard.*

こそ attaches to a noun and turns a flat statement into a pointed one. {{anata||あなた}}は{{ganbaru|masu|頑[がん]張[ば]りました}} just reports a fact — you worked hard, end of sentence. Swap は for こそ and the sentence stops being neutral: it singles {{anata||あなた}} out, as if there were other candidates for the credit and you're ruling every one of them out but this person. That's the whole job of こそ — precisely this noun, not some other one.

## How it works

The pattern is simple: **Noun + こそ**. こそ takes the seat that は (or が, or を) would otherwise occupy — you don't stack it on top of them. It works on people, things, times, anywhere a noun can sit at the front of a sentence.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}こそ{{v-hontou||本[ほん]当[とう]}}の{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}です。
```

*He is a true friend, if anyone is.*

Here {{kare||彼[かれ]}} isn't just being described — the sentence is answering an unspoken "who is actually a true friend?" and {{kare||彼[かれ]}} is the answer, full stop. That's the flavor こそ always carries: an implied lineup of candidates, with the noun before こそ walking away as the clear winner.

こそ also shows up glued onto から, and this combination is common enough to know cold: からこそ means "precisely *because*," pointing at a reason and insisting it's the real one.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}からこそ、{{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}}たい。
```

*Precisely because I'm busy, I want to rest.*

Without こそ, {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から{{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}}たい just states cause and effect. Add こそ and you're pushing back on an assumption — maybe someone expects that being busy means you *can't* rest, and you're insisting the opposite: busy is exactly *why* you need the break.

## Rules and exceptions

- こそ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it attaches to. You will never see `私はこそ` or `友達をこそ` — pick one or the other.
- こそ needs something to push against. It reads oddly on a sentence with no implied contrast or correction floating in the background — save it for moments where you're singling one thing out *from* others, not just stating a plain fact.
- こそ is register-neutral. It doesn't make a sentence more or less polite; です/ます still does that work on its own.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}こそ{{majime||真面目[まじめ]}}です。
```

*She is the one who's genuinely diligent.*

> Watch the difference between こそ and simply raising your voice on は in English. こそ isn't stress or volume — it's a grammatical word doing the singling-out, so it shows up in writing exactly the same way it does in speech.

## Contrast

Put は and こそ side by side and the gap is easy to feel.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}です。
```

*Today is busy.*

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}こそ{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}です。
```

*Today, of all days, is busy.*

The は version is a plain report — nothing special about today. The こそ version implies other days weren't like this, or that today was supposed to be the easy one, and instead it turned out to be the busy one. Same words, same です ending, completely different weight.

That's really all こそ does — it doesn't change tense, it doesn't change politeness, it just points a finger. Later on you'll meet さえ, which points a finger in the opposite direction: it flags an extreme example ("even this") rather than the definite winner こそ picks out. For now, when you want to insist on one noun over every alternative, こそ is the tool.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}こそ{{arigatou||ありがとう}}。
```

*No, thank *you*.*
caution_notes: こそ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it attaches to — never stack it on top of those particles.
からこそ means "precisely because," not "even though" — it doubles down on a reason rather than conceding it.
こそ reads oddly without an implied contrast; use it only when you're singling one noun out from real or assumed alternatives.
こそ does not affect politeness — です/ます still control formality on their own.

items.explanation_markdown:
You had one of those days. Meetings stacked on meetings, the train was late twice, and by the time you got home you realized you never sat down to eat. Not "skipped a snack" busy — *forgot breakfast existed* busy. That's the feeling さえ is built for: it doesn't just say something didn't happen, it says something so basic that its absence proves how bad things really were.

さえ attaches to a noun and means **even** — but not the casual "even" you'd use for a mild surprise. It marks the single most basic, most expected item on a list and says: not even *that* one. Everything harder than it is implied to have failed too. English does something similar when you say "I didn't even open my email today" — you're not really talking about email, you're using it as proof of how little else got done.

That's the intuition to hold onto: さえ isn't primarily about the noun it's attached to. It's a comment on everything else, delivered through the one item small enough to make the point unmissable. Pick the wrong item and the sentence stops working — "even the CEO showed up" only lands as extreme if the CEO is genuinely the person least likely to show; swap in someone who shows up every week and the whole sentence falls flat. さえ is honest that way: it only works when the noun really is the low bar.

## How it works

さえ sits right after the noun it's marking, and here's the part that trips people up: it *replaces* the particles that would normally mark subject or object — は, が, を all get pushed out. さえ takes their spot instead. There's no version where you keep the old particle and add さえ next to it; the noun only gets one marker, and さえ wins that slot.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}{{asagohan||朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}{{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}}さえなかった。
```

*I was so busy I didn't even have time to eat breakfast.*

Notice {{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}} (じかん — the word for time) has no を or が in front of it. さえ took that slot. The sentence isn't just "I didn't have time" — it's naming *time to eat breakfast* specifically as the most basic thing you'd expect to have, and saying you didn't even have that. Everything you'd normally need more time for — the actual work, the actual errands — is left for the listener to imagine as even further out of reach.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{kanji-word||漢[かん]字[じ]}}さえ{{shiru|nai|知[し]らない}}。
```

*He doesn't even know kanji.*

Same shape: {{kanji-word||漢[かん]字[じ]}} (かんじ) is the noun, さえ replaces what would have been を after {{shiru||知[し]る}} (しる — to know), and the whole sentence reads as "kanji is the baseline you'd expect him to have, and he's below it." If you were describing someone's Japanese level and wanted to make clear it's close to zero, this is the sentence that does it in five words instead of a paragraph.

There's also a stronger version: さえも. It's the exact same job, just louder — you reach for it when even さえ feels too mild for how extreme the example is.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{okane||お金[かね]}}さえも{{motsu|te|持[も]って}}{{iru-exist|nai|いない}}。
```

*She doesn't even have money.*

Money not existing is already a strong claim about how bad things are; さえも underlines it. In practice さえ and さえも are interchangeable in most sentences — さえも just leans harder on the surprise, the way stressing the word "even" with your voice does in English. Neither one is more correct than the other; it's a volume knob, not a grammar switch. If you're not sure which to pick, plain さえ is the safer default — さえも is the one you reach for on purpose, when the plain version already feels too weak for the moment.

## Rules and exceptions

The particle-replacing behavior only applies to は, が, and を — the ones whose entire job is marking subject or object and carry no meaning of their own. Particles that carry their own meaning, like に (at/to) or で (at/by), don't get evicted; さえ stacks on top of them instead (にさえ, でさえ). You won't need those combinations yet, but it's worth knowing さえ doesn't erase every particle it meets — only the three that were just pointing at the noun anyway, with nothing else to say.

> さえ needs a noun to attach to. If what you actually want to mark is an entire *action* — "he didn't even try" rather than "he didn't even have money" — you're reaching for a different tool than the one covered here; don't force さえ onto a verb directly.

This is one of those places where the textbook rule is clean but the temptation to bend it is real — English "even" attaches to almost anything, verbs included, so the instinct to do the same in Japanese is strong. Resist it here; keep さえ anchored to a noun and build the sentence around that noun instead of trying to translate word for word.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}は{{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{namae||名[な]前[まえ]}}さえ{{wasureru|ta|忘[わす]れた}}。
```

*My friend even forgot my name.*

This is the shape learners get wrong first: they leave は or を sitting next to さえ out of habit — something like `友達は私の名前をさえ忘れた`. That を doesn't belong there. さえ already did its job of marking the noun; stacking the old particle back on top of it is redundant and reads as a mistake, not extra emphasis. The fix is simple once you see it: whichever particle さえ is replacing, just drop it and let さえ stand alone.

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{tesuto||テスト}}は{{kantan-n4||簡[かん]単[たん]}}で、{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}さえ{{wakaru|ta|分[わ]かった}}。
```

*That test was easy; even a child understood it.*

Here さえ is doing something slightly different — instead of marking an absence, it's marking the low end of a scale of ability. A child is the last person you'd expect to understand something, so if even they did, the test really was easy. Same particle, same logic, flipped from negative to positive: さえ doesn't care whether the sentence is "didn't happen" or "did happen," only that the noun it's attached to is the least likely candidate for whatever the verb describes. That's genuinely the whole rule — once you can name the "least likely candidate" in a scenario, さえ tells you exactly where to put it, and the rest of the sentence takes care of itself.

## Contrast

You already know こそ for emphasis — it singles out one item and says *this one, specifically, for sure*. さえ and こそ can look like cousins because they both replace は/が/を on a noun, but they're pointing in opposite directions. こそ picks the item you're *most* confident about; さえ picks the item you'd *least* expect to fail.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}こそ{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}を{{suru|masu|します}}。
```

*Today, of all days, I will do my homework.*

こそ here is a promise: out of every day you could pick, today is the one it's actually going to happen. It's confident, forward-looking, almost stubborn — "today, unlike every other day, I mean it." Compare that to what さえ does with the same day and the same homework, just a different outcome:

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}、{{shukudai||宿[しゅく]題[だい]}}さえ{{suru|nai|しなかった}}。
```

*Today I was so busy that I didn't even do my homework.*

Swap こそ for さえ in that first sentence and the meaning flips completely — from "today is the day I finally will" to "today wasn't even good enough for the bare minimum." Same slot, same particle family, opposite emotional weather. If you mix them up, you don't get a small nuance shift; you get the sentence claiming the opposite of what happened, so it's worth pausing for a beat before you pick one.

```jp
{{konshuu||今[こん]週[しゅう]}}は{{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}、{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}さえ{{kakeru-call|nai|かけなかった}}。
```

*This week I was so busy that I didn't even make a phone call.*

That's the pattern doing its actual job: naming the smallest, easiest thing on the list and showing that even it didn't happen. It's a small particle carrying a lot of weight — one word standing in for a whole week you'd rather not describe in detail.

Hold onto that shape — once you meet さえ〜ば later, you'll see this same noun-marking さえ start pulling double duty inside a conditional, but that's a lesson for another day.
caution_notes: さえ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it marks — never stack the old particle back on top of it.
さえ attaches to a noun, not directly to a verb; it can't be used to mark an entire action on its own.
さえ and さえも are interchangeable in most sentences — さえも simply lands harder on the surprise.
さえ and こそ both replace は/が/を on a noun, but こそ marks confidence in the best case while さえ marks failure at the easiest case — swapping one for the other flips the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
You want to convince your friend that money is honestly the only thing standing between them and the trip they keep talking about — not the time off, not the planning, not their nerve, just the money. Every other excuse they've floated this week gets waved away; this is the one that actually blocks the door. In Japanese you reach for さえ〜ば, the pattern that names that one single thing and shrugs off everything else.

```jp
{{okane||お金[かね]}}さえ{{are||あれ}}ば、{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```
*If you just had the money, you could travel.*

That さえ is the same word you already met on its own, doing extreme-example work — *{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}さえ{{shiru|te|知[し]って}}{{iru-exist||いる}}* ("even a child knows"). Paired with a ば-form verb, though, it stops pointing at an extreme case and starts drawing a line: meet this one condition, and everything downstream of it is fine. Nothing else in the sentence gets to argue. It's a stronger, narrower claim than a plain "if" — a plain ば-conditional just describes one path among several; さえ〜ば insists there's only one path that matters.

## How it works

さえ attaches directly after a noun, and the verb after it takes its ば-form — the same ば you already use for ordinary "if" sentences, just with さえ wedged in front to say "as long as *just* this."

```jp
{{ganbaru||頑[がん]張[ば]る}} → {{ganbaru|stem|頑[がん]張[ば]れ}}ば
```

Swap in さえ before that ば-form and the meaning tightens from a general "if you try hard" to "as long as you *just* try hard — nothing more is needed." Nothing about the ば itself changes; さえ is simply riding in front of a conditional form you can already build on your own.

When the condition itself is an action rather than "if only I had this noun," さえ moves onto the verb's masu-stem, right before {{suru|stem|すれ}}ば. This is the shape you'll see most often in real speech, because most conditions people actually name are things to *do*, not things to *own* — study, rest, wait, try. Learners tend to reach for the noun pattern first because it's the one that gets taught first, but the verb pattern is doing more of the daily work once you start listening for it.

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}さえ{{suru|stem|すれ}}ば、{{shiken||試[し]験[けん]}}に{{v-goukaku||合[ごう]格[かく]}}{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```
*As long as you just study every day, you'll pass the exam.*

Notice what the sentence is quietly refusing to say: it isn't claiming studying is easy, or that nothing else matters in life. It's claiming that, of everything that could go into passing this exam, daily study is the one piece that's load-bearing. Take that piece away and the rest collapses; keep it, and the rest doesn't need to be perfect. That's the real intuition behind さえ〜ば — it's less about the size of the requirement and more about which requirement is the last one standing between you and the outcome.

```jp
{{sukoshi||少[すこ]し}}{{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}}さえ{{suru|stem|すれ}}ば、{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}に{{naru-become|masu|なります}}。
```
*As long as you just rest a little, you'll feel better.*

Same shape again — {{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}} is the masu-stem of {{yasumu||休[やす]む}}, so さえ sits between the stem and {{suru|stem|すれ}}ば exactly the way it did with {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}. Once you've drilled that one seam, さえ〜ば stops feeling like a new pattern and starts feeling like a small attachment you bolt onto ば-conditionals you already know. The stem itself never changes shape for さえ — you're not conjugating anything new, just inserting a particle into a slot that was always there.

## Rules and exceptions

The condition さえ marks has to be singular and real. Stacking a second さえ into the same clause to cover two conditions doesn't add them together — it just reads as a sentence that lost track of what it was arguing. Pick the one fact that's actually doing the work and say only that. If a situation genuinely has two independent requirements, さえ〜ば is the wrong tool; you'd need a plain list of conditions instead, without さえ narrowing either one.

> さえ〜ば and plain さえ look identical at a glance, but drop the ば and you've silently switched patterns. `お金さえある` with nothing after it just states "even money exists" — an extreme example, not a minimum requirement. The ば is what turns さえ from "even" into "as long as."

さえ〜ば also leans on the condition still being open. It works for things that could still go your way — study time still ahead of you, money you could still get. If the exam already happened and your friend already failed it, `勉強さえすれば良かった` reaching back at a closed door needs a different, past-tense shape than the plain さえ〜ば you're learning here; for now, keep さえ〜ば pointed at conditions that haven't been decided yet.

One more sharp edge: さえ〜ば doesn't promise the result is *guaranteed*, only that the named condition is *sufficient* in the speaker's mind. Someone else might disagree that money alone gets your friend on a plane — さえ〜ば is a claim about what the speaker believes is enough, not an objective law of the universe.

Politeness isn't a problem here either way: さえ〜ば sits comfortably in both casual conversation and formal speech, and nothing about it contracts or softens the way some other patterns do. You'll hear it from a teacher explaining an exam requirement just as readily as from a friend complaining about money, with the same shape both times.

## Contrast

You already know plain さえ for extreme examples — "even X," no ば, no minimum bar, just a case so far out that if it applies, everything milder must apply too.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}さえ{{wakaru|masu|分[わ]かります}}。
```
*Even a child understands.*

```jp
{{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}}さえ{{are||あれ}}ば、{{daijoubu-desu||大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]です}}。
```
*As long as I just have time, I'll be fine.*

Line one says a child clears a low bar — proof that something is easy enough for anyone. Line two says time is the *only* bar left standing — proof that everything else is already handled and this single thing is what's missing. Same word, opposite job: one measures how extreme an example is, the other measures how little is actually required.

It helps to notice what each sentence is silently comparing against. Plain さえ is always measuring against a scale of difficulty — a child is near the easy end, so if even they can do it, anyone further up the scale can too. さえ〜ば isn't measuring difficulty at all; it's measuring completeness, checking off the last item on a short list of requirements.

```jp
{{jisho||辞[じ]書[しょ]}}さえ{{are||あれ}}ば、{{kotoba||言[こと]葉[ば]}}が{{wakaru|masu|分[わ]かります}}。
```
*As long as I just have a dictionary, I'll understand the words.*

Swap さえ〜ば for plain さえ in that last sentence and you'd get something closer to "even a dictionary — [and yet I still don't understand the words]," an entirely different, mildly frustrated sentence. The ば is doing almost all of the meaning here, which is worth sitting with the first few times you write one of these. When you're not sure which reading a sentence you hear is going for, listen for what comes after さえ: a ば-form verb means "as long as," anything else — a period, another particle, silence — means "even."

## Closing thought

Once you can hear さえ〜ば as "name the one thing, and only that thing," a lot of everyday bargaining in Japanese — with teachers, with friends, with yourself — starts making more sense. It's the pattern people reach for when they want to cut a messy situation down to a single, negotiable variable. Hold onto that narrowing instinct: you'll meet a stricter, more formal cousin of it soon in のみ.
caution_notes: さえ〜ば and plain さえ (the "even" sibling you already know) share the same word, but only the version paired with a ば-form verb draws a minimum-requirement line — drop the ば and you're back to a plain extreme example.
さえ attaches to a noun directly, but to a verb's masu-stem (not the dictionary form) when the condition is an action, right before すれば.
さえ〜ば only works while the condition is still open to happen — it doesn't reach back to fix something that's already been decided.
Stacking a second さえ into one clause doesn't combine two conditions; keep the sentence pointed at exactly one thing.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in the lobby of a friend's company, waiting while they finish a call. A small sign by the elevator catches your eye: {{shain||社[しゃ]員[いん]}}のみ{{tsukaeru|masu|使[つか]えます}}. You can guess most of it — {{shain||社[しゃ]員[いん]}} is the staff, {{tsukaeru|masu|使[つか]えます}} is "can use" — but that middle word, のみ, is doing something specific. It's not decoration. It's telling you, flatly, that this elevator has exactly one group of people who are allowed near it, and you are not one of them.

You could read the same sign a dozen different ways in casual speech — "just staff," "staff and nobody else," "sorry, employees only" — but whoever printed that sign didn't reach for any of those. They reached for one tight, formal word that does the whole job by itself.

## How it works

のみ means "only" or "nothing but," and it attaches straight onto a noun — no particle, no conjugation, nothing in between. Noun + のみ, and that noun becomes the one and only thing the sentence is willing to allow.

```jp
{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}の{{iriguchi||入[いり]口[ぐち]}}は{{shain||社[しゃ]員[いん]}}のみ{{tsukaeru|masu|使[つか]えます}}。
```

*Only employees can use the company entrance.*

Notice that のみ sits right where a particle like は or が might otherwise go, and the verb follows normally after it. You don't need to add anything to make the sentence work — のみ already carries the restriction on its own. Nothing before it, nothing after it, just the noun and the verb doing their normal jobs around it.

のみ also sits comfortably right before です, closing out a sentence the same way a regular noun would.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{resutoran||レストラン}}は{{genkin||現[げん]金[きん]}}のみです。
```

*This restaurant is cash only.*

Read that one out loud and you can hear why it works so well as signage: it's short, it's blunt, and there's no room to misread it. です is doing the same job it always does — wrapping up the sentence — and のみ has already done the work of narrowing "payment" down to one single option before です even gets there.

That's the shape you'll see most often: a rule, a policy, a sign — something written down, meant to be read rather than said out loud. A workplace posts a notice, a store prints a sign, an exam proctor hands out a printed instruction sheet, and every one of them reaches for のみ instead of anything looser.

```jp
{{shiken||試[し]験[けん]}}の{{aida||間[あいだ]}}は{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}のみ{{hanaseru|masu|話[はな]せます}}。
```

*During the exam, only Japanese may be spoken.*

Same pattern each time: take the one noun that's allowed, drop のみ right after it, and let the rest of the sentence — a verb, です, whatever you need — carry on exactly as it would without のみ there at all. The grammar around it never has to change shape to make room.

## Rules and exceptions

のみ is formal, written-register Japanese — it belongs to the same world as printed rules and official announcements, not to a conversation between friends. You'll meet it constantly in signs, contracts, and business writing, and almost never hear it in someone's casual speech about their own day.

> Don't reach for のみ when you're just chatting. Saying `これのみ食べた` to a friend about your lunch sounds like you're reading from a memo, not describing a sandwich.

That stiffness is the whole point of the word, not a flaw in it. A company doesn't want its entrance policy to sound warm and conversational — it wants it to sound like a rule, and のみ carries exactly that weight. Once you can hear that formality, you'll start noticing のみ everywhere: on ticket machines, in contracts, on the fine print under a store's opening hours.

This lesson only covers のみ attached directly to a noun, which is by far the form you'll need most at this level. It can also attach after other things in more advanced writing, but treat that as a different problem for a different day — for now, noun first, のみ right after it, nothing in between. Resist the urge to bolt it onto a verb the way you might with some other patterns; at this stage, keep it a noun's word.

## Contrast

You already know 以[い]外[がい] for "except" — it pulls one thing *out* of a group and leaves the rest standing. のみ does the opposite: it throws everything out except the one thing it names.

```jp
{{nichiyoubi||日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}です。
```

*Every day except Sunday is work.*

```jp
{{nichiyoubi||日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]}}のみ{{v-yasumi||休[やす]み}}ます。
```

*I only rest on Sunday.*

Same subject, same week, completely different shape of sentence. 以[い]外[がい] tells you what's left after removing one day from the group; のみ tells you that one day is all there is, full stop. Swap one for the other in either sentence and the meaning flips almost entirely — worth sitting with that pair until the difference feels automatic.

さえ makes a different kind of point. It picks an extreme example to prove how easy or how surprising something is — "even a beginner could do this." のみ never argues that way; it just draws a hard line around who's allowed in, with no interest in surprising you.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}は{{otona||大人[おとな]}}のみ{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```

*Only adults can do this job.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}は{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}さえ{{dekiru|masu|できます}}。
```

*Even children can do this job.*

Same job, same verb, and the two sentences say almost opposite things about how demanding the work is. {{otona||大人[おとな]}}のみ makes it sound like it takes real skill, something only a narrow group can manage; {{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}さえ makes it sound so simple that even the least likely candidate can pull it off.

Sign-language のみ and this さえ trick don't fight for the same space — you'll usually know which one you need from the tone of what you're writing, not from the vocabulary itself. If you're posting a rule, reach for のみ. If you're making a point about how easy or surprising something is, reach for さえ instead.

That elevator sign wasn't being rude. It was just doing what のみ always does — naming one group and closing the door on everyone else, briefly and without apology. Hold onto that flat, no-exceptions feel; you'll want it again once we get to ほかない, where "there's no choice but to" carries the same refusal to budge.
caution_notes: のみ is formal, written-register Japanese — using it in ordinary conversation sounds like you're reading from a notice board.
This lesson's のみ attaches directly after a noun with nothing in between; don't insert a particle before it.
のみ and 以外 point in opposite directions: 以外 removes one thing from a group, while のみ keeps nothing but that one thing.
Don't confuse のみ with さえ: さえ reaches for an extreme example to make a point, it doesn't wall off who's allowed to do something.

items.explanation_markdown:
It's past midnight and you're standing outside the station. The gate is shut, the trains have stopped for the night, and the one taxi that passed didn't slow down. Your phone is dead, so calling anyone is out. Home is a long way off on foot, but there is genuinely nothing else left to try. The Japanese sentence that fits this exact feeling is short:

```jp
{{aruku|te|歩[ある]いて}}{{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}ほかない。
```
*I have no choice but to walk home.*

ほかない takes a situation where every other option has been stripped away and names the one that remains. It isn't a preference and it isn't advice. It's the last door still open, and you're walking through it only because the rest are locked.

## How it works

The build is about as plain as N4 grammar gets. Take a verb in its plain **dictionary form** (the shape you'd look up in a dictionary — {{iku-v||行[い]く}}, {{matsu||待[ま]つ}}, {{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}) and attach ほかない straight onto the end. Nothing changes shape, nothing conjugates.

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}} → {{iku-v||行[い]く}}ほかない
```
*go → have no choice but to go*

The ほか in there is the ordinary noun meaning "other", the one you already know from {{hoka||他[ほか]}}の{{hito||人[ひと]}}, "other people". The ない on the end is just the negative of {{aru||ある}}, "to exist". Put literally, the phrase says "(doing this) — there is no other". No other road, no other move. Once that literal picture is in your head, the meaning stops needing to be memorised.

Here is the station scene filled out a little more:

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{tomaru|ta|止[と]まった}}から、{{eki||駅[えき]}}で{{matsu||待[ま]つ}}ほかない。
```
*Since the trains have stopped, I have no choice but to wait at the station.*

And a weekend version — the kind of Sunday where the plan quietly falls apart:

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}{{dakara||だから}}、{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{iru-exist||いる}}ほかない。
```
*It's raining today, so I have no choice but to stay home.*

For a polite context — speaking with a teacher or a customer, or writing a formal email — swap ない for {{aru|masu|ありません}}. The meaning is identical; only the register moves up.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}に{{ayamaru||謝[あやま]る}}ほかありません。
```
*I have no choice but to apologize to him.*

Those two endings, ほかない and ほかありません, are the entire toolkit you need here. There is no past-tense or negated version to learn for this course.

## Rules and exceptions

The attachment point is strict: a **plain dictionary-form verb**, and nothing else. Not the past, not the negative, not the polite ます-stem, and not a noun or a na-adjective standing on its own.

- `行ったほかない` — wrong; the past tense doesn't belong here
- `行きますほかない` — wrong; no polite stem in front of it
- `学生ほかない` — wrong; ほかない doesn't clip onto a bare noun like this

If what you want is "there's no choice but *this thing*" with a noun, you need a different construction. ほかない is built for actions, not objects.

> ほかない is not emotionally neutral. It carries a clear undertone of *this is not what I wanted*. If the outcome actually suits you, or you're choosing it freely, ほかない will sound strangely bleak. Keep it for the forced hand.

Because the reason for the trap usually matters, ほかない very often follows a から or ので clause, or a なら. The clause before explains why the other options are gone; the pattern delivers what that leaves you with.

```jp
{{dare-mo||誰[だれ]も}}{{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]ない}}なら、{{hitori-de||一人[ひとり]で}}{{suru||する}}ほかない。
```
*If no one comes, I'll have no choice but to do it alone.*

## Register and small variations

This is a formal pattern with a written feel. You'll meet it in newspaper opinion pieces, in reports, in a manager passing on a decision that's already been made. Between friends, Japanese speakers usually pick something lighter, so don't sprinkle ほかない through casual conversation.

You may also see は slipped in for weight: ほかはない. It's the same pattern with a little more stress on the "no other" part — nothing new, just a form to recognise.

When the situation is about redoing something from scratch, the pattern still simply clips onto the dictionary form:

```jp
{{mou||もう}}{{v-ichido||一[いち]度[ど]}}{{yarinaosu||やり直[なお]す}}ほかない。
```
*There's nothing for it but to start over once more.*

## Up against のみ

The closest thing you've already learned is のみ, the formal "only". Both narrow the field to a single item, so they can feel swappable — until you actually swap them and watch the meaning tilt.

のみ is a flat statement of fact: *this and nothing else*, with no feeling attached. It sits on a noun.

```jp
{{matsu||待[ま]つ}}のみだ。
```
*There is only waiting.*

ほかない sits on a verb and adds the resignation: *every other option is gone, so this one is forced on me*.

```jp
{{matsu||待[ま]つ}}ほかない。
```
*There's no choice but to wait.*

"There is only waiting" can be calm, even disciplined — an athlete steadying themselves before a result. "There's no choice but to wait" is someone who wanted to act and can't. Same corner, different feeling. Want the bare fact? Use のみ. Want the trapped feeling? Use ほかない.

## The one-line version

ほかない = plain dictionary verb + "and there is no other move" — the single option left standing once the rest have been ruled out. When we reach {{ue||上[うえ]}}で later, you'll see the other side of this: settling on a course *after* weighing everything, instead of being handed only one.
caution_notes: Attach ほかない only to a plain dictionary-form verb, never to a past, negative, or polite stem, and never to a bare noun or na-adjective.
Use only ほかない or the polite ほかありません; this course has no past or negated version of the ending.
ほかない carries a note of reluctance, so avoid it for an option you actually want or choose freely.
The pattern is formal and written-leaning, so reach for something lighter in casual conversation.

items.explanation_markdown:
You check the weather app, and the little train icon has gone red. A storm rolled through overnight, and the line into the city is dead. Someone asks why you are late, and you need to name the thing that caused the shutdown — not a person who decided it, but an event that forced it.

```jp
{{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}によって、{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{tomaru|ta|止[と]まった}}。
```

*The trains stopped because of the typhoon.*

That is によって. You take a noun — here {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}} — and attach によって straight onto it to say 'because of this', 'by means of this', or 'through this'. It points at the thing sitting behind an outcome.

## How it works

The structure is as plain as it looks: a noun, then によって. Nothing sits between them — no の, no な, no です. If you can name it as a noun, you can feed it in.

によって does four related jobs, and they all grow from a single idea: the noun is the source or the pivot of whatever follows.

**Cause.** An event or a force produces a result. This is the 'because of' reading, and you meet it constantly in news, announcements, and any moment you want to sound a little formal about a cause.

```jp
{{jishin||地[じ]震[しん]}}によって、{{takusan||たくさん}}の{{ie||家[いえ]}}が{{kowareru|ta|壊[こわ]れた}}。
```

*The earthquake destroyed many houses.*

In stiffer writing — signs, reports, official notices — によって tightens to により. It is the same word clipped short, not a new one: same meaning, drier tone, nothing else changes.

```jp
{{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}によって → {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}により
```

*'Because of the typhoon', then the same phrase in its formal form.*

**Means or method.** The noun is the tool or the process that gets something done. Here によって sits close to で ('with', 'using'), but it frames the noun as a whole procedure — a negotiation, a vote, a piece of research — rather than a single object in someone's hand.

```jp
{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}によって、{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{yotei||予[よ]定[てい]}}が{{kimaru|ta|決[き]まった}}。
```

*The new schedule was settled through the meeting.*

**The doer in a passive sentence.** When a sentence is passive and you want to name who actually performed the action, によって marks that person. The reason is bookish: older Japanese built its passives this way, and formal modern writing kept the habit. You see it most with verbs of making and writing.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{sobo||祖[そ]母[ぼ]}}によって{{sodateru|stem|育[そだ]て}}られた。
```

*She was raised by her grandmother.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{uta||歌[うた]}}は{{yuumei||有[ゆう]名[めい]}}な{{hito||人[ひと]}}によって{{tsukuru|stem|作[つく]ら}}れた。
```

*This song was made by a famous person.*

**'Depending on'.** The noun is a variable, and the rest of the sentence shifts as that variable shifts. This is the reading people miss, because English often leaves the second half implied. Japanese does not — the sentence has to end on something that moves, a word like {{kawaru||変[か]わる}}.

```jp
{{hito||人[ひと]}}によって{{iken||意[い]見[けん]}}が{{kawaru||変[か]わる}}。
```

*Opinions vary from one person to the next.*

## Rules and exceptions

The noun attaches bare. Learners fresh from drilling noun-modifying の sometimes write `地震のによって` — cut that の. It is always {{jishin||地[じ]震[しん]}}によって.

For the passive 'by', ordinary speech usually just uses に. If your teacher praises you, in conversation that is {{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{homeru|stem|褒[ほ]め}}られた, not {{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}によって{{homeru|stem|褒[ほ]め}}られた. Save によって for formal writing, or for verbs of creation like {{tsukuru||作[つく]る}} and {{kaku||書[か]く}}, where a plain に can read as a location rather than a person.

> により is not a casual option. It belongs to written and spoken formality: reports, ceremonies, the station announcement itself. Drop it into a chat with a friend and you sound like you are reading aloud from a manual.

```jp
{{jishin||地[じ]震[しん]}}により、{{takusan||たくさん}}の{{hito||人[ひと]}}が{{komaru|ta|困[こま]った}}。
```

*The earthquake left many people in difficulty.*

One more trap: によって in the 'depending on' sense needs a real outcome clause. 'Depending on the person' is not a finished thought in Japanese any more than in English — you have to say what actually changes.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know in this register is のみ, the formal 'only'. のみ and により surface in the same places — notices, forms, official writing — and both sound wrong across a dinner table. Their jobs differ: のみ narrows the field to a single option, while により points at a cause or a means.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{mondai||問[もん]題[だい]}}は{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}により{{nakunaru|ta|無[な]くなった}}。
```

*This problem went away through a meeting.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{mise||店[みせ]}}は{{genkin||現[げん]金[きん]}}のみ{{tsukaeru||使[つか]える}}。
```

*This shop takes cash only.*

Swap the two and the sentences break: `会議のみ無くなった` would say 'only the meeting disappeared', and `現金により使える` would say 'usable by means of cash', which is not what a sign wants to tell you. A quick check: if the English slot takes 'only', you want のみ; if it takes 'because of' or 'by', you want により.

## One line to keep

によって hooks onto a noun to name the cause, the method, or the doer behind an outcome — により when the register is formal. Later you meet {{ue||上[うえ]}}で, another buttoned-up connector, where the noun is a step you finish before moving on rather than the force driving the result.
caution_notes: Attach によって straight to the noun — write 地震によって, never 地震のによって.
により is only the formal, written contraction of によって; keep it out of casual conversation.
For 'by' in an everyday passive, plain に is normal (先生に褒められた); によって suits formal writing and creation verbs like 作る and 書く.
In the 'depending on' sense, によって still needs an outcome clause that actually changes, such as one ending in 変わる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're lacing up your shoes to run to the convenience store before it closes. Your sister leans out of the kitchen: the fridge is empty, can you grab milk? You're already going out the door. You don't want to make the trip twice, and Japanese has one word for exactly this 'since I'm heading there anyway' move: ついでに.

```jp
{{konbini||コンビニ}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ついでに、{{gyuunyuu||牛[ぎゅう]乳[にゅう]}}を{{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}くる。
```

*While I'm going to the convenience store, I'll pick up some milk.*

The main mission is the convenience store. The milk is a rider — something small you fold into a trip you were making regardless. That is the whole feel of ついでに: one primary action, and a second, lighter action that gets a free ride on it. The two are not equal partners, and that imbalance is the point.

## How it works

ついでに attaches in two ways, depending on what sits in front of it.

**Dictionary-form verb + ついでに.** The verb names the trip or task you're already committed to. Attach ついでに straight onto the plain dictionary form — nothing comes between them.

```jp
{{eki||駅[えき]}}まで{{aruku||歩[ある]く}}ついでに、{{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}を{{dasu||出[だ]す}}。
```

*While I'm walking to the station, I'll mail the letter.*

Walking to the station is happening no matter what. Mailing the letter is the passenger. Watch the order: the action you were already doing comes first, then ついでに, then the add-on. A comma after ついでに is normal and helps the reader feel the seam.

**Noun + の + ついでに.** When the occasion is naturally a noun — shopping, a walk, a work trip — join it with の.

```jp
{{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}}のついでに、{{toshokan||図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]}}で{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{kaesu||返[かえ]す}}。
```

*While I'm out shopping, I'll return the books at the library.*

Here {{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}} is the trip and returning the library books is the extra stop. {{suru||する}}-verbs give you a choice: you can treat 掃[そう]除[じ] as a bare noun (掃[そう]除[じ]のついでに) or use the full verb ({{souji-suru||掃[そう]除[じ]する}}ついでに). Both are fine and mean the same thing.

```jp
{{daidokoro||台[だい]所[どころ]}}を{{souji-suru||掃[そう]除[じ]する}}ついでに、{{reizouko||冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]}}も{{arau||洗[あら]う}}。
```

*While I'm cleaning the kitchen, I'll wash out the fridge too.*

The も on {{reizouko||冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]}} is doing quiet work — it says 'this one as well, on top of the kitchen.' ついでに and も are natural partners, because the pattern is fundamentally about adding one more thing.

## Rules and exceptions

**The add-on has to be the smaller thing.** ついでに only sounds right when the second action is minor next to the first. If the second action is really your main goal, a listener will be puzzled.

```jp
{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}から{{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}ついでに、{{suupaa||スーパー}}で{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{kau-v||買[か]う}}。
```

*On my way home from work, I'll buy vegetables at the supermarket.*

Going home is the big fixed event; buying vegetables is slipped inside it. Flip the weights — if the shopping were the real reason you left — and ついでに becomes the wrong tool.

**Same person on both halves.** ついでに is not 'two people doing things at the same moment.' Whoever makes the trip is the one who does the extra task.

**Both actions share one occasion.** You can't use ついでに to staple together two errands from different days or separate trips. It is one outing, one stretch of being out, with an opportunity taken inside it.

> After a verb, ついでに clamps directly onto the dictionary form. Learners who just met the noun pattern sometimes carry the の across and write `行くのついでに` — that extra の is wrong. Only nouns take の.

One honest note: in relaxed speech you'll sometimes hear the の dropped after a noun as well, as in `買い物ついでに`. It is casual and common, but の is the standard choice and the one to write.

## Contrast

Your recent particles — こそ, さえ, のみ — all *narrow* or *spotlight*. のみ in particular means 'only this, nothing else.'

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yuubinkyoku||郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]}}のみ{{iku-v||行[い]く}}。
```

*Today I'll go only to the post office.*

ついでに pulls the opposite way. It doesn't trim the list down to one; it adds a second thing onto the single trip you were already taking.

```jp
{{yuubinkyoku||郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ついでに、{{ginkou||銀[ぎん]行[こう]}}にも{{okane||お金[かね]}}を{{dasu||出[だ]す}}。
```

*While I'm at the post office, I'll also take out money at the bank.*

Same starting point — a trip to the post office — but のみ shuts the door on anything else, while ついでに props it open for one more stop. If you catch yourself reaching for 'only,' ついでに is not what you want.

```jp
{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ついでに、{{yakkyoku||薬[やっ]局[きょく]}}で{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{morau||もらう}}。
```

*While I'm going to the hospital, I'll get medicine at the pharmacy.*

The hospital visit is settled; the pharmacy is a few steps out of the way and costs you nothing extra. That is the situation ついでに is built for.

## Closing

ついでに = one trip you were making anyway, plus a small extra thing you fold into it. Attach it to a dictionary-form verb directly, or to a noun with の.

Hold onto this 'in the middle of an action' feeling. Soon you'll meet {{saichuu||最[さい]中[ちゅう]}}に, which sounds close in English but runs the other way — it's about being caught right in the thick of something, not about picking up a bonus errand on the side.
caution_notes: ついでに only fits when the two actions belong to the same outing — it cannot link errands done on separate trips.
The tacked-on action must be the minor one; if it is your real goal, ついでに sounds wrong.
Attach ついでに straight to a dictionary-form verb — writing 行くのついでに with an extra の is an error, since only nouns take の.
Keep one subject across both halves; ついでに never means two people acting at the same time.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are three days from moving into a new apartment. The agent slides a contract across the table, taps the signature line, and asks for your decision right now. You are not going to say yes on the spot. You want to read every clause first — the deposit, the notice period, the penalty for leaving early — and commit only once you have seen all of it. In a message to a friend you would use a plain, casual 'after' for this and move on. But a rental office is a formal room, and Japanese keeps a separate, more buttoned-up tool for exactly this thought: 'I will do the real thing, but only once this first step is properly finished.' That tool is 〜た上[うえ]で.

```jp
{{shorui||書[しょ]類[るい]}}を{{zenbu||全[ぜん]部[ぶ]}}{{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}上[うえ]で、{{kimeru-v|masu|決[き]めます}}。
```

*I will decide after I have read all the documents.*

Everything about the pattern is sitting in that one line. There is a finished first action — reading the documents — then the connector 上[うえ]で, then the action the sentence is really about: deciding. The first half is preparation you take on yourself. The second half is the payoff. 上[うえ]で tells your listener that the second thing is not happening loosely or by luck; it happens on the foundation of the first thing being done.

It helps to know where the phrase comes from. {{ue||上[うえ]}} is the word for 'up' or 'on top of', and this pattern is that image made abstract: the second action stands on top of the completed first one, the way a next floor stands on the one below. Once you see that picture, the formal 'on the basis of' sense stops feeling arbitrary.

## How it works

Put the first action into the plain past — the ta-form — and attach 上[うえ]で directly to it. The main clause follows.

```jp
{{yomu||読[よ]む}} → {{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}上[うえ]で
```

```jp
{{hanashiau||話[はな]し合[あ]う}} → {{hanashiau|ta|話[はな]し合[あ]った}}上[うえ]で
```

Here is the same move in slow motion:

- Start with the verb for the preparatory action: {{yomu||読[よ]む}}.
- Shift it to the plain past: {{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}.
- Attach 上[うえ]で with nothing in between: {{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}上[うえ]で.
- Add the main clause — the decision, the reply, the purchase.

The join is tight: no comma inside {{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}上[うえ]で, no particle, no breath.

Why the ta-form specifically? Because 上[うえ]で treats that first action as complete — not in progress, not skipped over, but genuinely wrapped up — and then stacks the second action on top of it. That is exactly why a dictionary form (`読む上で`) or a te-form (`読んで上で`) will not carry this meaning: neither of them says 'this part is already done.'

Since the first clause is groundwork, the two halves belong to the same person, and both are things that person chooses to do. Think of yourself giving a careful answer to something that matters — a job offer, an expensive purchase, a decision that affects your family. You do the checking first, on purpose, and your answer waits for it.

```jp
{{kazoku||家[か]族[ぞく]}}と{{yoku||よく}}{{hanashiau|ta|話[はな]し合[あ]った}}上[うえ]で、お{{kotae||答[こた]え}}{{suru|masu|します}}。
```

*I will give you my answer once I have talked it over properly with my family.*

```jp
{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}に{{kiku-v|ta|聞[き]いた}}上[うえ]で、{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}。
```

*I will take the medicine after checking with the doctor.*

The main clause does not have to point at the future. It often does, because you are usually laying out a plan, but you can just as easily report something you have already finished in this same deliberate, step-by-step way.

```jp
{{setsumei||説[せつ]明[めい]}}を{{kiku-v|ta|聞[き]いた}}上[うえ]で、{{v-moushikomi||申[もう]し込[こ]み}}ました。
```

*I applied after hearing the explanation.*

There is also a noun version, for nouns that name a process — a discussion, a survey, an application, an inspection. Add の, then 上[うえ]で.

```jp
{{chousa||調[ちょう]査[さ]}}の上[うえ]で、{{kekka||結[けっ]果[か]}}を{{tsutaeru|masu|伝[つた]えます}}。
```

*We will report the results after the investigation.*

## Rules and exceptions

What can sit in front of this 上[うえ]で is narrow: a ta-form verb, or a process noun plus の. Nothing else fits the slot.

> `読む上で` and `読んで上で` are both wrong for the 'having done X' meaning. It has to be {{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}上[うえ]で.

Both actions have to be deliberate and within your control, because the entire point of 上[うえ]で is that you arranged the order on purpose. It falls apart when the first 'action' is really something that happened to you — the weather turning, a train running late, a mistake you never meant to make. For those you want an ordinary 'after' or 'because', not this pattern.

```jp
{{shiken||試[し]験[けん]}}を受[う]けた上[うえ]で、{{kekka||結[けっ]果[か]}}を{{matsu|masu|待[ま]ちます}}。
```

*Having sat the exam, I will wait for the results.*

Sitting the exam is a chosen step; waiting is what follows from it. That is the shape 上[うえ]で is built for.

One more limit worth naming: the first clause is a single completed action, not an ongoing state. You would not use it for something like being tired or knowing a fact — those are conditions, not steps you finish and move on from. If you cannot picture a clean moment where the first action is over and the second one begins, the pattern is probably the wrong choice, and a simpler 'after' or 'because' will serve you better.

Register matters here as well. This construction is formal, and it leans written: contracts, official notices, business email, a measured spoken reply in a meeting. Part of why formal Japanese reaches for it is that it makes the groundwork explicit — it says the decision rests on a proper basis, that the right step was taken before the outcome. Drop the same phrase into a relaxed conversation and it sounds starched. Among friends, a plain 'after' gives you the same sequence with none of the stiffness.

> Do not mix this 上[うえ]で up with the plain, everyday 上[うえ]で that means 'on top of a surface' — {{tsukue||机[つくえ]}}の上[うえ]で{{kaku||書[か]く}}, 'to write on the desk'. That one needs a physical place and carries no sense of one action ending before another begins. Same two characters, unrelated grammar.

## Against ついでに

You already know ついでに, the 'while I am at it' pattern. It also lines up two actions, but it faces the opposite way. With ついでに, the first action is already happening for its own reasons, and you tack the second one on because it costs you almost nothing — you would never make a special trip just for it.

```jp
{{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}}のついでに、{{yuubinkyoku||郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]}}で{{kitte||切[きっ]手[て]}}を{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}}。
```

*While I am out shopping anyway, I will buy stamps at the post office.*

上[うえ]で is the mirror image. The first action is a step you take on purpose, precisely so the second one can be done properly.

```jp
{{nedan||値[ね]段[だん]}}を{{yoku||よく}}{{v-kangae||考[かんが]え}}た上[うえ]で、{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}}。
```

*I will buy it after thinking the price over carefully.*

Swap the two patterns and the meaning lurches. {{kaimono||買[か]い物[もの]}}を{{suru|ta|した}}上[うえ]で、{{kitte||切[きっ]手[て]}}を{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}} comes out sounding as though you treated a whole shopping trip as a formal precondition for buying stamps — a strange thing to claim. If the second action is a small add-on, you need ついでに. If the first action is a real prerequisite that you completed deliberately, you need 上[うえ]で.

There is a tone difference too. ついでに is light and a little informal — it works fine in casual speech, and it often carries a shrug, as if the extra task barely counts. 上[うえ]で is the opposite: it is weighty and careful, the language of someone signalling that they did not rush. Reaching for 上[うえ]で when you mean ついでに makes a trivial errand sound like a solemn procedure, and the reverse makes a serious step sound careless. Matching the pattern to how much the first action actually mattered is most of getting this right.

## One line to keep

A ta-form plus 上[うえ]で means 'having finished that, and on the strength of it, now this' — deliberate groundwork, then the real move, in a formal voice. Hold onto the timing, because the next pattern you will meet, {{saichuu||最[さい]中[ちゅう]}}に, marks the opposite moment: not once a step is done, but right in the middle of one that is still going.
caution_notes: Use only a plain-past (ta-form) verb or a process noun plus の before this 上で; a dictionary form or te-form is wrong for the 'having done X' meaning.
Both clauses must share one subject and be deliberate, controllable actions, not accidents or events like weather or delays.
The pattern is formal and mostly written; in casual conversation a plain 'after' is used instead.
This sequence 上で is unrelated to the everyday 上で meaning 'on top of a surface' despite the shared characters.
